paper: Onal & Esen, A Crank-Nicolson Approximation for the time Fractional Burgers Equation, Applied Mathematics and Nonlinear Sciences 5(2) (2020) 177-184, doi:10.2478/amns.2020.2.00023

open_questions.q: Does the paper's scheme retain its 8-significant-figure accuracy if the Caputo D_t^gamma is replaced by the Riemann-Liouville derivative (with the corresponding IC-consistency correction), or does the L1-discretized memory kernel silently commit the replication to Caputo semantics?
open_questions.basis: The paper (and our replication) uses the Caputo derivative with the L1 formula b_k = (k+1)^{1-gamma} - k^{1-gamma}. Caputo vs Riemann-Liouville differ by a term involving the initial condition; the L1 quadrature is standard for Caputo but is often reused for Riemann-Liouville with an initial-value correction. Whether the CN/L1 tridiagonal system in Section 2.1 remains consistent under that swap is not tested in the paper or in our replication.
next_steps: Re-derive the fully-discrete system with D_t^gamma interpreted as Riemann-Liouville (initial-value correction absorbed into the RHS) and re-solve Example 1 at gamma=0.5, M in {40,80,100}.
Compare error norms against our Caputo-based Table 1/2 values; any drift beyond floating-point noise identifies terms whose derivative-flavor is scheme-critical.
If they agree to 8 sig figs on manufactured solutions (which have u(x,0)=0 for Example 1, killing the correction), design a non-zero-IC test where Caputo and RL provably differ and re-check.

open_questions.q: What is the empirical temporal order of accuracy in Delta t as a function of gamma, and does it match the L1-theoretical O(Delta t^{2-gamma}) uniformly across gamma in [0.1, 0.9]?
open_questions.basis: The paper's Table 4 sweeps gamma at fixed N=120 but fixed Delta t; our replication reproduces those values to 8 sig figs but performs no Delta t refinement. The L1 scheme is theoretically O(Delta t^{2-gamma}), which degrades from ~O(Delta t^{1.9}) at gamma=0.1 to O(Delta t^{1.1}) at gamma=0.9. Whether the paper's CN wrapper preserves that rate --- especially at gamma close to 1 where the temporal error dominates --- is untested.
next_steps: Fix M large (say M=200) to make spatial error negligible; run Delta t in {1e-3, 5e-4, 2.5e-4, 1.25e-4, 6.25e-5} for gamma in {0.1, 0.5, 0.9}.
Fit log(L2-err) vs log(Delta t) and report the observed slope alongside the theoretical (2-gamma).
If observed rate is below theoretical for large gamma, investigate whether the CN averaging of the advection u u_x re-introduces an O(Delta t) term that the L1 formula alone would not.

open_questions.q: Does the CN/L1 tridiagonal formulation extend cleanly to a variable-order Caputo derivative D_t^{gamma(x,t)} u, and if so, is the tridiagonal structure preserved or does spatially-varying gamma couple neighbouring memory sums?
open_questions.basis: The paper handles constant fractional order gamma; the b_k coefficients are computed once and reused for all j. In variable-order fractional PDEs (increasingly common in viscoelasticity and anomalous transport), gamma depends on x (and possibly t and u), so each spatial node carries its own memory kernel. Whether the paper's Section 2.1 derivation survives that generalization --- and at what per-step cost --- is not addressed.
next_steps: Re-derive the fully-discrete system with gamma -> gamma_j (piecewise constant per node), tracking whether b_k stays diagonal or picks up j-dependence that breaks the tridiagonal solve.

Implement a smoothly varying gamma(x) = 0.3 + 0.6 x on Example 1's manufactured setup, check consistency by symbolic differentiation of the manufactured u against the variable-order operator, and measure error norms.
Benchmark against a fixed-order gamma = mean(gamma(x)) baseline to quantify the accuracy gain from variable order.

open_questions.q: How does the scheme behave when the exact solution develops a near-shock (steep gradient) --- does the CN averaging plus Caputo memory kernel produce sub-diffusive shock smearing, or does the semi-implicit advection introduce spurious oscillations?
open_questions.basis: All three manufactured test problems (u = t^2 sin(2 pi x), t^2 cos(pi x), t^2 e^x) are globally smooth and monotone-in-t; they never approach the shock-formation regime that motivates Burgers' equation in the first place. The fractional memory term is known to delay shock formation (sub-diffusive smoothing); whether the paper's L1/CN scheme captures that delay quantitatively, or whether it merely smears any steep gradient at any gamma, is not explored.
next_steps: Set nu small (say 0.01), gamma in {0.3, 0.7, 0.99}, initial condition u(x,0) = sin(2 pi x) with no forcing (f=0) --- the classical shock-forming Burgers test.
Track the maximum |u_x| through time; compare to a high-resolution reference solution obtained by an L2 discretization or spectral method.
Report shock-formation time vs gamma and whether the paper's scheme exhibits TVD-like behaviour or Gibbs-like oscillations near the forming shock.

open_questions.q: How does the paper's L1-based CN scheme compare in accuracy-per-cost to newer L2 / L2-1_sigma / L1-2 discretizations of the Caputo derivative on the exact same test problems?
open_questions.basis: The paper uses the classical L1 quadrature, which is O(Delta t^{2-gamma}) with an O(N_t) memory sum per time step. Since 2020, L2-1_sigma (Alikhanov) and L1-2 schemes deliver O(Delta t^2) uniformly in gamma at the same asymptotic cost. Whether the paper's headline errors (Tables 1, 2, 4) would improve materially under a modern discretization --- and whether the CN wrapper is the bottleneck --- is not discussed.
next_steps: Re-implement the same CN spatial/nonlinear treatment with the L1 memory sum swapped for L2-1_sigma (Alikhanov 2015) coefficients.
Re-run Example 1 Table 1 (M in {10,20,40,80}, gamma=0.5) and Table 4 (gamma sweep at N=120), tabulating L2 and L_inf errors alongside our reproduced L1 values.
Compute wall-clock cost per time step; report the accuracy-per-second Pareto front to quantify whether the 2020 paper's method is still competitive or superseded.
